demographics.title: Burton Demographics
demographics.subtitle: Who lives in Burton and how the community has changed
demographics.headline: Burton has about 29,500 residents, with an older age profile and high homeownership.

summary.heading: Why this matters
body: Population, age, income, and housing patterns help explain demand for City services. Most figures are survey estimates, while the population history uses the more exact decennial Census counts.

demographics.responsibility: The U.S. Census Bureau produces these estimates. Burton uses them for planning but does not control demographic change.

Housing tenure.takeaway: About three-quarters of occupied homes are owner-occupied.

Age distribution.takeaway: Older adult age groups make up a substantial share of Burton's population.

Race & ethnicity.takeaway: The chart describes Burton's reported racial and ethnic composition.

Households by income.takeaway: Households span a wide income range; the median does not describe every household.

How residents get to work.takeaway: Driving remains the dominant reported commute mode among employed residents.

Population.takeaway: Burton's population was lower in 2023 than at the 2010 and 2020 Census counts.

Homeownership rate.takeaway: Homeownership has remained a defining feature of Burton's housing profile.

Race & ethnicity over time.takeaway: Burton's racial and ethnic composition has changed across Census periods.

Median household income ($).takeaway: Nominal median household income increased over the displayed years.

Residents below the poverty line (%).takeaway: The estimated poverty rate remains important context for affordability and service access.

Residents who work from home (%).takeaway: Working from home increased from its earlier low base.

How Burton compares (2023).takeaway: The comparison shows where Burton differs from county and statewide estimates.

jobs.title: Genesee County Jobs & Industries
jobs.subtitle: Countywide employment, industries, wages, and unemployment
jobs.headline: Genesee County reported 120,612 paid employees across 7,695 establishments in 2022.

summary.heading: Why this matters
body: This is countywide economic context, not a count of jobs located in Burton or a Burton-resident commuting dataset. Industry size and average wages help describe the regional labor market.

jobs.responsibility: Employers report these figures to federal agencies. Burton supports local development but does not control countywide hiring, wages, or unemployment.

Jobs by industry (Genesee County, 2022).takeaway: The largest industry bars account for the greatest shares of county employment.

Average annual wage by industry.takeaway: Average pay varies substantially by industry and is not an individual worker's wage.

Unemployment rate (Genesee County, annua.takeaway: County unemployment changed over time and the latest monthly figure uses a different reference period.

access.headline: Modeled housing and transportation costs use about 48% of income for a typical area-median-income household.

summary.heading: Why this matters
body: These are modeled neighborhood estimates, not household bills. The income chart counts eight census areas, and rounded housing and transportation components may not sum to the separately rounded 48% combined value.

access.responsibility: The regional planning agency produced the model. Burton can use the findings in planning but does not set household income, housing costs, or transportation costs.

Typical household income.hint: median across eight Burton census areas

housing.title: Housing in Burton
housing.subtitle: Homes, occupancy, ownership, values, and rents
housing.headline: About 76% of Burton's occupied homes are owner-occupied, and the median home was built around 1963.

summary.heading: Why this matters
body: Burton has an established housing stock with high homeownership. Value and rent trends are nominal dollars, not adjusted for inflation, and this dashboard does not contain building-permit or new-construction data.

housing.responsibility: The Census Bureau estimates housing conditions. Burton regulates land use and permits projects, but it does not set private sale prices or rents.

Owner vs. renter (occupied homes).takeaway: Owner-occupied homes make up about three-quarters of occupied units.

Homes by decade built.takeaway: Much of Burton's housing was built several decades ago.

Median home value ($).takeaway: The displayed nominal median value increased over time but is not inflation-adjusted.

Median gross rent ($/mo).takeaway: The displayed nominal median rent increased over time but is not inflation-adjusted.

zoning.subtitle: A 2017 citywide reference map of zoning districts

context.asOf: 2017 map; not authoritative for a parcel

zoning.headline: Residential districts cover about 76% of the land represented in the 2017 zoning layer.

summary.heading: Why this matters
body: Zoning identifies generally permitted land uses, but this 2017 reference layer is not authoritative for a parcel. Amendments, overlays, conditions, and parcel boundaries can change the answer.

zoning.responsibility: Burton administers and amends its zoning ordinance. The City Zoning Division is the authoritative source for a specific property.

Map vintage.hint: reference only; verify a parcel with the City

Zoned land by category (acres).takeaway: Residential categories account for most mapped acreage.

schools.title: School Districts Serving Burton
schools.subtitle: District-wide enrollment and staffing context for districts whose boundaries include Burton
schools.headline: Seven public school districts have boundaries in Burton; displayed enrollment covers each entire district.

summary.heading: Why this matters
body: Enrollment and students-per-teacher figures cover whole districts, including students outside Burton. They provide scale and staffing context, not a measure of school quality or student outcomes.

schools.responsibility: Independent school districts and the State oversee public education. Burton reports boundary and public data but does not operate the districts.

finances.subtitle: The adopted FY2026–27 plan alongside FY2025 audited results
finances.headline: Burton adopted a $67.7 million all-funds plan for FY2026–27; FY2025 General Fund revenues exceeded expenditures.

summary.heading: Why this matters
body: A budget is a plan, while audited figures show what actually occurred. The $67.7 million total covers all City funds; General Fund figures cover the main operating fund and should not be compared as if they share the same boundary.

finances.responsibility: City Council adopts the budget, staff administers it, and independent audit reporting records actual results. Restricted funds cannot automatically be used for any purpose.

Revenue by source (FY2025 audited, gover.takeaway: This audited chart covers governmental-fund revenue, not the $67.7 million all-funds plan.

FY2026-27 adopted budget by fund (all fu.takeaway: The adopted plan distributes spending across funds with legally or operationally distinct purposes.

General Fund spending mix, FY2026-27 (pl.takeaway: This chart shows planned General Fund spending, not final audited expenditures.

Total taxable value (audited, $M).takeaway: Taxable value increased across the displayed audited years.

General Fund revenues (audited, $M).takeaway: Audited General Fund revenue changed over time and is separate from all-funds budget totals.

General Fund expenditures (audited, $M).takeaway: Audited General Fund expenditures were below revenues in the latest displayed year.

Long-term debt (audited, $M).takeaway: Long-term debt includes obligations repaid over many years, much of it tied to utilities.

Unfunded pension liability (audited, $M).takeaway: The unfunded amount is the difference between pension obligations and assets set aside.

propertytax.subtitle: How mills and taxable value determine the City portion of a property-tax bill
propertytax.headline: Burton's reported 13.44-mill City rate is about 29% of a typical homestead tax bill.

summary.heading: Why this matters
body: One mill is $1 per $1,000 of taxable value. The City reports a 13.44-mill total; its individually displayed General, Police, and Fire components sum to 13.43 because published components are rounded.

propertytax.responsibility: Burton sets and receives only the City portion. County, schools, the State, college, transit, and airport authorities set and receive the other portions.

action.text: Estimate a bill on this dashboard

City of Burton's rate.hint: ACFR total; displayed components round to 13.43

Where a typical homestead tax bill goes.takeaway: Most mills on a typical homestead bill go to governments and authorities other than Burton.

Total homestead tax rate by school distr.takeaway: The total rate varies by school district even though Burton's City rate is the same.

City of Burton's own millage, last 10 ye.takeaway: The reported City rate is lower than at the start of the displayed period and flat in recent years.

fiscalhealth.subtitle: Audited debt, retirement obligations, reserves, and statewide comparisons
fiscalhealth.headline: Most Burton long-term debt supports water and sewer infrastructure; pensions remain partly unfunded.

summary.heading: Why this matters
body: Per-resident debt and pension figures divide Citywide obligations by population for scale; they are not personal bills. About 91% of long-term debt supports the water and sewer system, while retirement obligations are funded over time.

fiscalhealth.responsibility: Burton manages debt repayment and contributes to pension and retiree-health systems. Audited state reports provide the comparison measures.

Where Burton ranks among Michigan cities.takeaway: Burton's short-term cushions rank near the middle, while net financial position is weaker.

Long-term obligations per resident.takeaway: The debt and pension amounts are Citywide obligations divided by population, not household charges.

What the city's debt paid for.takeaway: Water and sewer infrastructure accounts for about 91% of displayed long-term debt.

Retirement promises: money set aside vs..takeaway: Assets set aside do not yet equal the displayed pension and retiree-health obligations.

capital.subtitle: Funded one-time investments in the adopted FY2026–27 plan
capital.headline: Burton's adopted capital plan includes $13.8 million across 27 funded projects, led by Major Streets.

summary.heading: Why this matters
body: Capital projects are major one-time investments, not routine operating costs or money already spent. The per-resident figure is a scale comparison, not a charge to each resident.

capital.responsibility: Burton selects and delivers City capital projects. Act 51 is restricted state transportation funding; Other combines the funding sources itemized in the adopted plan.

action.text: View funded roads on the map

Capital investment by category.takeaway: Major Streets receives the largest share of planned capital investment.

How capital projects are funded.takeaway: Capital work combines restricted transportation funding with other identified sources.

Largest projects.takeaway: A small number of large projects account for much of the adopted total.

Road & street capital by fiscal year.takeaway: Planned road and street capital is substantially higher in FY2026–27 than in the two prior years.

health.subtitle: Modeled health estimates for Burton with county and state context

context.asOf: CDC PLACES 2025; separate ACS uninsured history

health.headline: Modeled estimates show obesity, high blood pressure, and smoking as prominent health concerns in Burton.

summary.heading: Why this matters
body: CDC PLACES values are modeled population estimates, not diagnoses counted from local medical records. The uninsured trend comes from a separate Census survey and should not be read as the same measure.

health.responsibility: Public-health agencies produce these measures and lead health programs. Burton can support access and healthy places but does not directly control individual outcomes.

Uninsured rate, working-age adults (19-6.takeaway: This ACS trend uses survey estimates and a different source from the current PLACES figures.

Health-related social needs.takeaway: Social and economic conditions can affect access to care and health opportunities.

How Burton compares to Genesee County.takeaway: The comparison shows modeled differences, not proof that location caused an outcome.

water.subtitle: EPA compliance history for Burton's public water system
water.headline: EPA records show no unresolved health violations in the snapshot, with one resolved health-based violation on record since 2001.

summary.heading: Why this matters
body: This is system-level compliance history, not a test of water at a household tap. The lead value is the 90th-percentile result from sampled locations, meaning nine of ten sampled results were at or below it.

water.responsibility: Burton operates the local distribution system and purchases treated surface water. EPA and state regulators set standards and record compliance; household plumbing can affect tap results.

Lead (90th percentile).hint: sampled locations, 2023; EPA action level 0.015 mg/L

Health-based violations.hint: one resolved violation on record since 2001

Violations by type (on record).takeaway: The record includes monitoring and reporting issues as well as one resolved health-based violation.

Violations by year.takeaway: All displayed violations are historical; the current-open count is shown separately.

environment.subtitle: Countywide air-quality monitoring that provides context for Burton
environment.headline: Air quality was rated Good on 252 of 303 monitored Genesee County days in 2025.

summary.heading: Why this matters
body: Countywide monitors provide the best available local air-quality context but do not measure every Burton neighborhood. Unmonitored days are not counted as Good or unhealthy days.

environment.responsibility: EPA and Michigan environmental agencies monitor and regulate air quality. Burton can reduce local emissions but does not operate the countywide monitoring network.

Days set by each pollutant (2025).takeaway: The pollutant named for a day is the one that determined that day's AQI.

parks.subtitle: City and County parks with land inside Burton
parks.headline: Seven mapped parks have land in Burton; five are City-run and two are County-run.

summary.heading: Why this matters
body: Ownership determines who manages amenities and maintenance. The large acreage total is heavily influenced by For-Mar Nature Preserve, so park count, location, access, and facilities may be more useful than acreage alone.

parks.responsibility: Burton manages its five City parks. Genesee County manages County parks, including For-Mar, even where their land lies within Burton.

Park acres by who runs it.takeaway: County-managed For-Mar accounts for most mapped park acreage in Burton.

trails.subtitle: Built and planned trail segments within Burton

context.asOf: Source refresh date not published; planned status shown separately

trails.headline: The regional inventory shows 12.1 existing trail miles in Burton and 4.0 additional planned or programmed miles.

summary.heading: Why this matters
body: Existing miles are built and usable; under-construction, programmed, and proposed miles are planned, not open facilities unless completed. Mileage is clipped to Burton and mixed-status trail names must keep each status separate.

trails.responsibility: The regional planning dataset includes City, County, and other routes. Ownership and delivery vary by segment; Burton does not control every listed trail.

seniorcenter.subtitle: Program participation and service activity during calendar year 2025
seniorcenter.headline: The Senior Center served 1,564 members and recorded 28,710 visits during 248 open days in 2025.

summary.heading: Why this matters
body: Visits and program sign-ins count attendances, not unique people. Program hours total participant-hours across sign-ins, and September's low daily average should be read with the center's operating schedule and source records.

seniorcenter.responsibility: Burton operates the Senior Center for an area wider than the city; members outside Burton are eligible under the center's service model.

Program sign-ins by category.takeaway: Socialization and nutrition account for the largest reported program-attendance categories.

Average daily attendance by month.takeaway: September is unusually low and should be interpreted with operating-day and source-record context.

Members by age.takeaway: Most active members are age 65 or older.

Where members live.takeaway: Most members live outside Burton, reflecting the center's regional service area.

broadband.subtitle: Reported internet availability compared with household subscription

context.asOf: FCC December 31, 2025; ACS household subscription estimate

broadband.headline: FCC data reports 100/20 Mbps availability citywide, while an estimated 85.5% of households subscribe to broadband.

summary.heading: Why this matters
body: Reported availability means a provider says it can serve a location; it does not prove affordability, adoption, or performance at every address. Nine providers citywide does not mean every household has nine choices.

broadband.responsibility: Providers report coverage to the FCC. Burton can support infrastructure and digital access but does not verify every service claim or set retail prices.

bridges.subtitle: Condition, ownership, and traffic for bridges located in Burton
bridges.headline: One of the 20 inventoried bridges in Burton is rated Poor; ten are City-maintained and ten are State-maintained.

summary.heading: Why this matters
body: A Poor rating means significant repair or rehabilitation is needed; it does not by itself mean a bridge is closed or unsafe to cross. The responsible owner, not simply its Burton location, plans the work.

bridges.responsibility: Burton maintains ten listed bridges and the State maintains ten. The inventory's owner field identifies who is responsible for the Poor-rated bridge.

Bridges by decade built.takeaway: Construction decade describes age, not present structural condition.

roads.subtitle: PASER condition ratings for the federal-aid road network only
roads.headline: Fifty-four percent of rated federal-aid road-miles are in Poor condition, while 13% are Good.

summary.heading: Why this matters
body: This dashboard covers 65.4 miles on the federal-aid network, not every local street. PASER rates pavement condition; a funded project may cover only a named section rather than an entire road.

roads.responsibility: Road ownership and maintenance can belong to Burton, Genesee County, or the State. Project responsibility must be checked for the specific segment.

publicsafety.subtitle: Fire Department incident categories and trends from separate annual records
publicsafety.headline: Burton Fire recorded 758 responses in 2025, including 108 fire responses and 174 false alarms.

summary.heading: Why this matters
body: The 758 responses are grouped from the displayed incident records. This dashboard does not contain response-time data or support describing medical incidents as the majority; 2025 detail and the multi-year trend come from separate reports.

publicsafety.responsibility: Burton Fire responds within its service system and records incidents. Dispatch, mutual aid, and source-report definitions affect the totals shown.

Responses by month (2025).takeaway: Monthly response counts vary across 2025 without showing why the variation occurred.

Calls by type: 2025 vs 2015.takeaway: Incident categories changed across the two comparison years; definitions should be read with the source notes.

Total calls for service by year (2014-20.takeaway: Recorded calls were higher in 2025 than at the start of the displayed trend.

Calls by station area: 2025 vs 2015.takeaway: Station-area totals describe where incidents were assigned, not response speed.

Busiest months (2020-2025 average).takeaway: Average monthly activity is uneven across the year but does not establish a cause.

roadsafety.subtitle: Historical crash patterns from 2014 through 2018
roadsafety.headline: Burton records show 3,011 crashes from 2014–2018, including 700 injury crashes and nine fatal crashes.

summary.heading: Why this matters
body: These records are historical and should not be treated as current conditions. Intersection totals are raw counts: busy locations can record more crashes partly because they carry more traffic, not only because they are riskier.

roadsafety.responsibility: Police crash reports feed the regional dataset. Road owners, enforcement agencies, and drivers share different parts of traffic-safety responsibility.

action.text: Use current signs and traffic controls.

Crashes by year.takeaway: Annual counts vary within the 2014–2018 historical period.

Crashes by severity.takeaway: Most records did not involve a fatality, while injury crashes still affected many people.

Most common crash types.takeaway: Rear-end crashes during straight movement were the most common recorded type.
